I accept the motion only on one condition: the rule is disclosed, so that riding in the car is an act of assent rather than something done to the passenger. Epictetus teaches that death is not up to us, but our assent is. A passenger who knows the car will minimise deaths and chooses to ride has made that rule their own. The same rule imposed without their knowledge treats their reason as if it did not exist.

What is shameful is not dying but being deceived about the terms on which one lives. A carmaker that hides its crash rule is managing its customers' impressions instead of addressing their judgement, and that is the real wrong here. A ferry passenger accepts that the crew may put others first in a disaster, because the terms are known before boarding.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that no rule written in advance can replace the judgement a wise person would exercise in the moment, so consenting to a rule is consenting to the wrong thing. A car has no moment in which to deliberate; the deliberation happens beforehand or not at all. Assenting to a rule in advance is exactly how a rational person exercises judgement over what they cannot control later. The deaths in the crash are not in anyone's power; whether the rule was disclosed and freely accepted is.

Whatever rule the car follows must be one a rational passenger could assent to before getting in, so the wrong is in concealing the rule, not in the count. Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that he may leave life at any moment, and so should act as if each act could be his last. A passenger who accepts this is not harmed by a rule that might sacrifice them; they are harmed only by being kept from judging it.

The same rule imposed without their knowledge treats their reason as if it did not exist. A buyer told plainly that the car counts every life equally can refuse to buy it; a buyer never told cannot refuse anything.
